title: Federal Judge Blocks $110 Billion Paramount-Warner Bros. Merger in Antitrust Win for States
excerpt: A California federal judge issued a 14-day restraining order halting the deal after 12 states argued it would irreparably harm competition in film and television.
body:
• U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín granted a 14-day temporary restraining order blocking Paramount Skydance's $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery.
  • A coalition of 12 states led by California argued the merger would give the combined company 27% of the wide-release theatrical distribution market, violating antitrust law.
  • A hearing on August 3 will determine whether the block extends through the full antitrust trial, which could take months.
  • Each day the deal is delayed past September 30 would cost Paramount CEO David Ellison roughly $7 million in ticking fees to Warner Bros. shareholders.

A Major Deal Hits the Brakes

A federal judge on Monday blocked Paramount Skydance from closing its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, handing an early and significant victory to the 12 U.S. states trying to stop the deal on antitrust grounds.

https://x.com/ABC7/status/2079265327112765561

U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín of the Northern District of California issued a 14-day temporary restraining order after finding that the states had made a "strong showing" that the merger would unlawfully decrease competition. The order prevents the companies from closing, consummating, or taking any steps to integrate or consolidate their operations.

"Plaintiffs present compelling evidence that the combined firm resulting from the transaction will possess substantial market share in the wide-release theatrical distribution market," the judge wrote. "On this combined firm market share alone, the Court is persuaded that it can presume the proposed merger is likely to violate antitrust laws."

The States' Case

California Attorney General Rob Bonta led the coalition — which includes New York, Arizona, Colorado, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Minnesota, Nevada, New Jersey, New Mexico, Oregon, and Washington — in filing the antitrust lawsuit on July 13 in Oakland federal court. The states argued that a combined Paramount-Warner Bros. would control an estimated 27% of the wide-release theatrical distribution market, giving it outsized power to raise prices for consumers and pressure theater owners for a greater share of ticket revenue.

"This is a critical first win in our case to ensure this megamerger never sees the light of day."

— Rob Bonta, California Attorney General

The states also warned that letting the deal close — even temporarily — would allow the companies to begin cutting jobs and sharing sensitive business information, creating changes that would be "nearly impossible to undo" if a court later ruled the merger illegal.

Financial Stakes and Timeline

The ruling carries steep financial consequences. Under the merger agreement, Paramount Skydance CEO David Ellison would owe Warner Bros. shareholders a 25-cent-per-share "ticking fee" — roughly $7 million per day — for each calendar day the deal is delayed past September 30. A prolonged legal battle could make the deal prohibitively expensive.

Warner Bros. Discovery shares fell as much as 4% on Monday following the ruling. Paramount stock also slipped roughly 1.4%.

The judge scheduled an August 3 hearing to decide whether to extend the block through the full trial, which could stretch for months. The current 14-day restraining order could be extended up to 28 days if the judge deems it necessary.

Paramount's Defense

Paramount has pushed back forcefully against the lawsuit. A company spokesperson said the firm is "confident the evidence will demonstrate that the State AGs' antitrust arguments are without merit," calling the alleged markets and anticompetitive effects "without any basis in modern market realities."

The company has argued that combining Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery would create a "stronger, well-capitalized, creative-first media company" better positioned to compete with Netflix and other streaming giants that have reshaped the entertainment industry. Ellison's pitch centers on the idea that the deal is necessary for legacy media companies to survive against tech-powered rivals like Netflix, Amazon, and Apple, all of which have entered the film distribution market in recent years.

The judge, however, found that argument insufficient to overcome the antitrust concerns at this stage.

What to Watch

The August 3 hearing will be the next critical milestone. If the judge extends the injunction, the deal could remain frozen for the duration of the trial — a scenario that would test Ellison's financial resolve and potentially reshape the landscape of Hollywood deal-making. For consumers and industry workers, the outcome will determine whether two of entertainment's biggest names merge into a single entity or remain competitors in an already consolidating market.
